title: Can bipartite maximal fractional matching be found in sublinear-in-degree rounds?
formal:
Is there a deterministic LOCAL algorithm and a function $f(\Delta)=o(\Delta)$ that, on every simple bipartite graph of maximum degree at most Delta, outputs a maximal fractional matching within f(Delta) rounds, independently of n? Each edge e receives a nonnegative rational weight x_e, agreed upon by its endpoints. Require $\sum_{e
i v}x_e\le1$ for every vertex v, and for every edge uv require $\sum_{e
i u}x_e=1$ or $\sum_{e
i v}x_e=1$. The bipartition is supplied as an input two-coloring, nodes know n and Delta, and identifiers are distinct O(log n)-bit integers.
answer_criterion: Construct a uniform algorithm with a degree-only bound whose ratio to Delta tends to zero, or prove that no such deterministic algorithm exists. An additive log-star n term, an almost-maximal solution, or a lower bound only for nonbipartite graphs does not settle this target.
context:
A fractional matching divides one unit of capacity at each vertex among its incident edges. Maximality means that no single edge can have its weight increased without exceeding an endpoint’s capacity. It does not mean that the total edge weight is as large as possible.

For example, on a star one can place the entire unit on a single leaf edge or divide it equally among all leaf edges. Both assignments saturate the center and are maximal, even though many leaves are unsaturated. Allowing fractions gives the algorithm ways to share capacity that do not exist for ordinary integral matching.

Bipartiteness supplies a globally consistent division into two sides, and the card gives that division to the algorithm. This can remove symmetry obstacles that occur when a vertex does not know which role it should play. Nevertheless, neighboring choices still have to agree on edge weights and achieve exact saturation somewhere along every edge.

Approximate saturation is a different requirement: leaving a small amount of unused capacity at both endpoints violates the condition on that edge. The known linear-degree lower bound on general graphs therefore cannot simply be combined with an approximation algorithm or transferred to the supplied-bipartition setting. The source specifically leaves this bipartite case open.
why: I include this because it asks whether relaxing discrete choices to fractional ones changes the intrinsic time needed for local coordination, once a bipartition is available. The constraints are simple, but exact maximality makes the question stronger than approximately solving a packing problem.
definitions: LOCAL uses synchronous rounds with unbounded messages along input edges and unrestricted local computation. Rational weights have finite encodings; there is no imposed output-bit bound. The algorithm must work for every identifier assignment and every valid supplied degree bound. The little-o statement concerns Delta tending to infinity and must hold uniformly over all graph sizes. Vertices output weights for all incident edges, with exact endpoint agreement.

progress.text: Åstrand and Suomela give local algorithms for approximating covering and packing problems, including the linear-degree maximal-fractional-matching upper bound used in subsequent work.
Göös, Hirvonen, and Suomela prove that o(Delta) rounds are impossible for maximal fractional matching on general graphs. This does not resolve the bipartite question as stated.
Suomela’s open-problem list explicitly asks for o(Delta) rounds on bipartite graphs and conjectures that the answer is negative.
